w:r.w:t: In the modern fast changing digital age, the issue of citizen safety and immediate awareness of the incident has become topical among citizens and law enforcers. The classic crime mapping tools are largely based on proven crime records, which misses a huge gap of managing unconfirmed incident reports and offering proactive safety information. SafeVision is created to solve these problems as an intelligent AI-driven web-based safety and incident management platform that helps to bridge the gap between reported incidents and actionable safety intelligence.

As opposed to traditional systems that only process the verified crimes, the SafeVision will process the First Information Reports (FIRs) but will always draw a line between reported cases and confirmed crimes. The platform allows citizens, administrators and law enforcement agencies to monitor, predict and act on safety issues in a single interface.

The architecture of the platform includes three different levels of access SuperAdmin, Admin and User; it is written in FastAPI to provide a high-performance backend, React.js to have a responsive frontend interface, and MySQL to have secure and scalable data storage. SuperAdmins have complete control over the system including user control, registration of the administrator, validation of the FIR data, and access to classified records. Both SuperAdmins and Admins use a multi-layered AI-based prediction engine that integrates Poisson probability modeling with Random Forest classification to facilitate both the support of manual and multi-crime prediction by date, area, and incident type.

The user interface offers interactive incident heatmaps which display route suggestions that prioritize safety along with real-time navigation and contact location sharing through messaging features and automated alerts for high-risk zones and expected incidents which users receive through email and browser notifications

The organization conducts testing and validation activities while developing the system to confirm its performance through ongoing accuracy testing and responsiveness testing and reliability testing. Early feedback demonstrates that SafeVision combines artificial intelligence with geospatial analytics and automated document processing and real-time alert systems to create a comprehensive public safety platform that provides predictive capabilities

Explanation of Important Constructs of the Application Domain
Grasping the theoretical bases of SafeVision necessitates scrutinizing several crucial constructions that collectively comprise the intellectual core of intelligent safety administration systems

Public safety governance operates through technological tools which handle data and structured processes to conduct risk assessment and danger reduction activities. The previous systems operated through event response procedures which followed emergency occurrences while current systems employ data analysis and predictive modeling to prevent incidents from happening. SafeVision achieves this concept through its system which documents incidents and provides users with tools to predict threats through data analysis to enhance public safety

Predictive forecasting uses historical and current data to assess potential future threats. The system operates under the belief that past patterns will assist in predicting future events although researchers must manage challenges which arise from both data quality concerns and ethical research obligations. SafeVision uses two methods for its operation which include Poisson probability modeling to deliver precise percentage forecasts and Random Forest
classification to identify complex patterns and categorize different risk levels

Geospatial awareness involves using location-specific data together with mapping technologies to investigate spatial patterns and their relationships across multiple areas. The security management system uses geospatial intelligence to identify dangerous areas while creating incident maps and assessing how threats vary across different locations. Decision-making depends on location data because incidents tend to gather in specific areas instead of spreading out evenly across space. SafeVision utilizes heatmaps to show dangerous areas while using radius-based security assessments and Haversine distance calculations to determine which incidents fall inside a user's notification range

Notification systems deliver emergency alerts to users through immediate and practical safety information. The system connects analysis with operation because it transforms data understanding into useful direction. Good notice systems need to show the right information using clear language which requires users to keep reading until they reach full understanding of the situation. The system uses location-based filtering and cooldown protocols to prevent repeated alerts while sending out alerts through browser pushes and electronic mail and in-app warnings. The system includes direct routing hyperlinks which enable users to go directly to detailed content whenever they need it

Statistical likelihood modeling uses mathematical equations to determine event probabilities based on existing data. Security systems use the Poisson distribution as a standard method to predict rare events throughout various time intervals. The technique provides a reliable approximation because real-world conditions present more complex challenges. SafeVision uses this model to calculate risk assessment percentages which include the risk of a crime occurring in a particular time and location. The method establishes standardization through probabilistic

Machine learning classification uses historic examples to create data groups through pattern identification. Advanced statistical models enable the detection of intricate data connections which traditional statistical methods cannot identify. In SafeVision, a Random Forest Classifier uses previous incident data which includes location and offense type and time of day and season to divide risk levels into three categories: Elevated, Moderate, and Minimal.
Random Forest implementation improves model accuracy by reducing overfitting, which makes it suitable for security datasets that follow structured formats

The risk appraisal system uses incident data to generate one numerical value which indicates the risk level present in that specific situation. The system offers more detailed safety assessments through its ability to assess danger levels for different safety classes. The risk assessment for SafeVision results from combining essential risk factors through their respective weightings which assign 35% to transgression frequency and 30% to immediacy and 15% to gravity and 10% to trajectory and 10% to temporal factor. The rating system operates to evaluate both the number of incidents and their timings and their evolving patterns

SafeVision uses a three-level prediction system to maintain system reliability and continuous operational system functioning. The system combines different techniques into a defined sequence instead of using only one technique. The first level uses the Poisson model to create accurate probability predictions when there is sufficient available data. The system switches to the Random Forest model when the main method fails because of insufficient data. The system employs a basic label encoding system as a backup method to ensure users receive some form of risk assessment, which functions as a mandatory requirement. The tiered structure provides continuous system operation while it prevents failures through its ability to handle different types of data situations

The Multi-Tiered AI Estimation Unit uses three methods to estimate risk through its primary method of Poisson Probability and its secondary method of Random Forest and its Legacy method

Retrieve historical occurrences; determine lambda from occurrences per interval; return FAIL if lambda is zero; compute P(X>=1)=1-e^(-lambda); convert to percentage; round to single decimal spot; return hazard proportion

Collect authorized incident records; prepare and encode categorical fields; construct time/season features; part data; train Random Forest with balanced sets; assess framework; store framework, encoders, and scaler

Fetch framework artifacts; derive features from zone, incident type, time, and day; encode and scale features; estimate likelihoods and class; relate class to Low/Medium/High; return hazard tier and certainty
The system allocates scores through pre-set zone hazard tiers and incident seriousness tiers; it merges the scores which lead to High/Medium/Low; and it provides a low-certainty backup outcome

The first step of the process involves testing Poisson; if it produces a value the system will link to the hazard tier while registering the outcome; if Poisson fails the system will proceed to test Random Forest; if Random Forest also fails the system will use Legacy backup; the system will always generate an estimation result

Fetch incidents by zone or radius; gauge quantity, newness, seriousness, progression, and timing inputs; apply weights 35/30/15/10/10; compute hazard rating and safety rating; apply decay and safe-by-default stipulations; return factor breakdown.

Password hashing, token expiry, account lockout, 2FA being mandatory with privileged users, and Lahore location validation were all tested. The security layer was reliable and invalid areas were rejected. The key weakness is that geocoding relies on the external Nominatim service.

The three-layer prediction pipeline had an overall prediction accuracy of 78.2 percent, weighted precision of 0.79, weighted recall of 0.78, and zero system failure rate, and an average response time of 234 ms. The common crime patterns were most accurately predicted and the rare categories least
Risk Scoring and Safety Score Validation
Expert judgment was significantly correlated with the weighted risk score, and the Pearson

correlation and mean difference between the two were 0.87 and 3.8 points respectively. This renders the score applicable in relative comparisons despite the fact that it is not to be regarded as an absolute measure of public-safety

EasyOCR has always been most successful with Urdu FIR scans, with a maximum success of 94.2 percent on high-quality images, 86.7 percent on medium-quality images, and 72.3 percent on low-quality images. The processing time also became much faster with the help of GPU acceleration and it must be applied in manufacturing

Browser push delivery was 92.0% successful, email was 97.5% successful and integrated delivery was 99.0% successful. Duplicate alerts were avoided by the cooldown system and email was the most trusted channel

The system reached the 100-user mark without much strain and the average response time of 100 concurrent users was 289 ms and the error rate of 0.2%. The deterioration of performance started after this since the bottleneck was created by the database

Simple navigation was self-intuitive. Almost all participants were successful in registration, viewing safety scores, and uploading an FIR to the administrator, and the primary source of usability conflict was with notification permissions

SMS fallback, improved handwriting OCR and database read replicas should be added as short-term work. Medium term work should increase the coverage of the cities and enhance the prediction engine. The mobile packaging with Capacitor, real-time data sources, and more comprehensive analytics may also be considered in the long-term work
